transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Well, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in today is that I just feel like I’m always, always moving from one thing to the next. I really can’t just idle, you know? It's like my engine is always running. 

I've been a customer service rep for a long time, and I usually found ways to deal with it over the years. I'd keep busy, maybe pace a little if I was on a headset with a customer, just doing whatever I needed to do to keep moving. But they recently changed our whole work setup at the company. They brought in all these new protocols and changed how our stations are arranged, and honestly, this new setup has made it a lot harder to hide. 

Before, I could kind of mask the fact that I'm constantly shifting around and needing to be in motion, but now I'm right out there in the open. It's just glaringly obvious to everyone that I can't just sit quietly in neutral. I'm always bouncing to the next activity, and I think my supervisor is starting to notice because I just can't power down and blend in anymore. It's exhausting, to be honest with you, just constantly feeling this push to be doing the next thing and the next thing...
Did you experience this need to be constantly moving when you were a child?

Oh, absolutely, yes. I mean, looking back on it, this whole feeling of having a motor running inside me, it’s been around long, long before this recent job change. I was just thinking about this the other day, actually, because my sister was going through some old boxes of our parents' stuff, and she found some of my old report cards from grade school. It was wild reading them, really. 

Every single teacher, I mean, from second grade all the way up, they all wrote pretty much the exact same things. They’d say, you know, "He’s a bright boy, very capable," but then right after that, it was always, "but he’s so careless with his assignments," or "he rushes through things." And the talking! Oh man, they were always writing notes home about how I talked out of turn, how I’d just blurt things out in the middle of a lesson because I couldn't hold the thought in, or I couldn't just sit there quietly. 

They were constantly having to remind me to stay with my work, to stay at my desk. I remember Mrs. Gable in fourth grade—she actually moved my desk right next to hers because I was always wandering over to the pencil sharpener or looking out the window or bothering the kid next to me. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s just that, you know, when you’re an adult, you figure out little tricks to hide it, or you find a job where pacing around is okay, but back then, in a classroom? It was a real problem. I was just always, always on the go, and they just couldn't get me to settle down and focus on one thing for more than five minutes.
Did you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finished speaking when you were in school?

Well, yes, in school for sure, like I was saying, I’d just blurt things out. But honestly, it’s not just something from back then, it’s something I still do all the time right now at work. And I really, really don't mean to be rude, you know? I consider myself a polite person, I really do. But it's like... okay, for example, we have these pods at work now, right? With the new setup. So I can hear everything. And if I hear a couple of my coworkers, say, two desks over, and they're working through a complicated customer problem—maybe it's a billing issue, or a return that's outside the 30-day window, whatever it is—I can hear them struggling to figure out the protocol. 

And before I even realize I'm doing it, before I can stop myself, I just jump right in. I'll just call out the answer from my desk before they've even finished explaining the problem to each other, and definitely before anyone actually asked for my help. It’s like the answer just bubbles up in my throat and I have to get it out immediately. I can see them kind of jump, or look at me like, "We weren't talking to you," and I always feel terrible afterward because I know it comes off as intrusive or like I'm a know-it-all. But in the moment, it just feels so urgent to give them the answer. I just can't seem to hold it in and wait for a natural pause, or wait to be invited into the conversation. It just comes flying out of me.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking, like interrupting others or intruding on conversations, in situations outside of talking or speaking?

You know, I don't really think so. I mean, I've really been racking my brain trying to think if I do things like that—just acting on impulse without thinking about it first, outside of the whole talking thing, I mean. Because the talking, like I said, that's a huge thing for me. I just blurt things out, jump into conversations, all of that. But when it comes to actually *doing* things, like physical actions or intruding on people in other ways, I don't really see myself doing that. 

I mean, I'm trying to think of an example. Like, if someone is using the copier at work, I don't just walk up and push their papers out of the way to do mine, you know? I'll wait my turn. Or if someone is walking ahead of me in the hall, I don't just shove past them because I'm in a hurry. I might feel antsy, I might be pacing a little while I wait for the copier, or walking really fast behind them, but I don't actually physically intrude on what they're doing. 

I guess what I'm saying is, the impulsivity for me seems to be mostly verbal. It's the words that just fly out before I can stop them. But with my actions, I feel like I have a little more control, or at least I'm not just doing things without any thought at all. I might be moving a lot, like I mentioned with the pacing and not being able to sit still, but it's not like I'm just randomly grabbing things or jumping into the middle of a physical activity someone else is doing. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to that one. It's really just the talking and the blurting things out that gets me into trouble. I just don't have that same kind of impulsive action when it comes to other things. It's kind of funny how that works, isn't it? Like, my mouth is disconnected from my brain, but my body still kind of knows the rules, mostly.
Do you often find it hard to finish tasks or projects because you lose focus or get distracted?

Well, yes, actually. That's a huge thing for me, especially lately with this new setup at work. It's like... okay, so in customer service, especially when you're doing the online chats, which is mostly what I do now, there's a very specific way you're supposed to handle things when a customer gets angry or when the issue is beyond what a regular rep can authorize. We call it an escalation. 

So, say a supervisor comes over—or, well, messages me now, since we're in the pods—and gives me a rundown of what to do. They'll say, "Okay, first, issue the partial refund, then document the exact error code in the customer's main file, send an email to the logistics team to intercept the package, and finally, set a reminder to follow up with the customer in 48 hours." It's usually three or four steps like that, right? And I hear them, I really do, and I'll say, "Got it," and I dive right in. 

I'll get that partial refund processed immediately, no problem. I'm right on top of that first part. But then... I don't know what happens. It's like my brain just decides the crisis is averted because the customer is happy with the refund, or maybe another chat dings in and grabs my attention, or I just start thinking about what I'm going to have for lunch. Whatever it is, I just kind of... drift away from the rest of the instructions. 

I'll leave the file open on my screen, meaning to put the notes in, but then an hour goes by, and I haven't done it. The email to logistics? Forget it, it just completely falls out of my head. And the follow-up reminder never gets set. I just leave the whole back-end part of the process sitting there, completely unfinished. And it's not that I'm trying to be lazy or defiant, I just literally lose the thread of what I was supposed to be doing. I'll be working on three other things, thinking I'm doing a great job, until my supervisor messages me later and says, "Hey, did you ever finish documenting that escalation from this morning?" And then I get that sinking feeling in my stomach because I realize I only did the very first step and completely abandoned the rest of it. It happens all the time, and it's so frustrating because I know the steps, I just can't seem to hold my focus long enough to get through all of them before something else pulls me away.
Do you often fidget with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's actually kind of a running joke with some of the people I work with, though I guess it's probably not always that funny to them. But yeah, even when I’m really trying my best to just sit there and look completely calm and collected, my body is just... doing its own thing. 

Like, under my desk? My foot is just constantly bouncing. Up and down, up and down, like a little jackhammer. I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until I notice my monitors are sort of vibrating, or one of the other reps in the pod next to me gives me a look. And it's not just my feet, either. My hands are always looking for something to do. Like, whenever we have our team meetings—we do these weekly huddles in the conference room to go over our call metrics and new return policies and all that—I always bring a pen with me. You know, just in case I need to write something down, which I usually don't, but I have it anyway. And without even being aware of it, I'll just sit there clicking the top of the pen. Click, click, click. 

I'll be sitting there, looking right at the manager, thinking I look totally engaged and perfectly professional and still, but my thumb is just going to town on that pen. It's completely subconscious! Usually, it takes someone actually leaning over and whispering, "Hey, can you stop doing that?" for me to even realize I'm making a noise. It's just like my energy has to leak out somehow, you know? If I'm forced to just sit there in a chair for a twenty-minute meeting, my foot or my hands are going to find a way to keep moving, whether I want them to or not. I've tried sitting on my hands, or crossing my ankles really tight under the chair to lock my legs in place, but honestly, within five minutes I've uncrossed them and the foot is right back to bouncing again. It's just really hard to just... be still.
Do you have trouble waiting for your turn in lines or when doing group activities?

Well, yeah, I do, actually. It's funny you ask that because it's something I've noticed a lot more lately with how things are structured at work now. You know, we have these team huddles, like I mentioned before, and then there's the help queue when we need a supervisor's assistance during a chat. And waiting... waiting is just really, really hard for me. It's like my skin starts to crawl, honestly. 

Take the team huddles, for example. The manager will go around the room, asking for updates or letting people share some kind of difficult customer interaction they had that week. And I know my turn is coming up. I know I'm like, third in line. But sitting there while the first two people are talking... I just get so antsy. I start shifting in my chair, and I can feel this pressure building up in my chest, like I just need to get my part out right that second. I catch myself almost leaning forward, opening my mouth, wanting to just jump in and say my piece before I'm even called on. I have to actively bite my tongue sometimes because the urge to just blurt out my update and be done with it is so strong. It's not that I don't care what my coworkers are saying, it's just the physical act of waiting my turn feels almost impossible sometimes.

And it's the same thing with the help queue on our chat system. When you have a really angry customer online and you need a supervisor to step in and authorize something big, you put your name in this digital queue. And you can see your spot. You're number four, then number three, then number two. And I will literally sit there, refreshing the screen, checking it over and over and over again. I know checking it doesn't make it go any faster, but I just can't stop myself. The customer is waiting, I'm waiting, and the whole time I'm just practically vibrating in my seat, staring at that little number on the screen, wishing I could just bypass the line and get what I need right then. It's just this overwhelming feeling of restlessness, like I can't just peacefully exist in a state of waiting. It has to happen now, you know?
Do you often find yourself saying or doing things when you're upset that you later regret?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I definitely get upset, don't get me wrong. You can't work in customer service for as many years as I have and not get upset. It's just the nature of the beast, right? Especially with the online chats we do now. People are so much braver when they're just typing at a screen instead of talking to a real human being on the phone. Just the other day, I had this guy—he bought one of our refurbished smart home hubs, the older model, not even the new one—and he was absolutely losing his mind because it wouldn't sync with his third-party security cameras. Which, if he had read the manual, it clearly states it doesn't support that anyway.

But anyway, he's typing all in caps, calling me every name in the book, telling me I'm useless and the company is a scam. And sure, my blood pressure goes up. I'm sitting there at my pod, and I can feel my face getting hot, and I'm definitely frustrated. But I don't... I don't actually lash out or type something back that I'd get fired for. I think after all these years, I've got this built-in filter for that kind of thing. I might take a deep breath, or maybe I'll mutter something under my breath to myself, like alright buddy whatever you say, but I don't actually say or do things I regret. I don't fly off the handle. I just type back the standard corporate response about understanding his frustration and looking for a resolution. 

Even outside of work, like with my wife or my neighbors. If I get mad, I usually just kind of withdraw a bit or go watch TV to cool down. I'm not really a yeller, and I don't have those moments where I just explode and then have to go apologize later because I said something terrible. I might be a lot of things, and I know I get distracted and fidgety like we were just talking about, but keeping my temper in check is actually something I'm pretty good at. I just let people vent and stick to the script, you know?
Do you often have trouble organizing your tasks and activities?

Organizing? No, not really. Actually, that's one of the things I think I've got a pretty good handle on, to be honest. I mean, at work, it's all pretty much laid out for you anyway, so there's not much organizing I even have to do myself. We use this customer management system—it’s a customized version of Zendesk that corporate rolled out maybe three, three and a half years ago. Which, by the way, was a complete nightmare to learn at first because the old system had all our quick-reply macros right there on the left side of the screen, and the new one buried them in these tiny drop-down menus that you have to click three times just to find the standard shipping policy. 

But anyway, the system basically organizes my entire shift for me. The chats just come in automatically. Ping, ping, ping. I don't have to sit there and decide what task to do next or prioritize anything because the routing software does all that. You just take the next chat in the queue, help the customer, log the disposition code—you know, whether it was a return, or technical support, or just a billing question—and then you're right back in the pool for the next one. It’s very sequential, so I never really feel lost about what I'm supposed to be doing.

And then at home, I wouldn't say I struggle with it either. My wife, she’s a very organized person. Honestly, maybe a bit too organized sometimes, but it works for us. We have this big dry-erase calendar right on the front of the refrigerator, and she color-codes absolutely everything. Blue marker for doctor's appointments, red for when the utility bills are due, green for when our daughter is bringing the grandkids over. So if I ever need to know what I'm supposed to be doing on a Saturday afternoon, I just look at the fridge. Plus, I set all our regular bills up on autopay a few years back. That was probably one of the best decisions I ever made, honestly. I highly recommend it if you haven't done it yourself, it saves so much hassle with buying stamps and trying to remember due dates. 

So, yeah... I mean, maybe if I was trying to run my own business from scratch or had to plan some massive project with a hundred moving parts, I might get a little overwhelmed, but for my day-to-day life? No, I don't really have any trouble keeping my tasks straight. I just follow the queue at work and the whiteboard at home, and it all gets done.
Do you find it hard to focus when you're reading or doing other quiet activities by yourself?

Yeah, actually, that is something I struggle with. Especially at work. You know, we have these longer coaching meetings every month—they call them 'quality assurance reviews'—where they pull you off the queue for like, forty-five minutes to an hour to go over your metrics. And they also send out these massive emails whenever they change a policy. 

Like just last week, they completely revamped the warranty protocols for those smart home hubs I was telling you about earlier. So they send out this PDF, and it's maybe four or five pages long, just dense, tiny text about what qualifies for a free replacement and what doesn't, and all the new disposition codes we have to use. And I sit there at my desk, and it's quiet, right? Because I'm in an offline status to review it. And I open the document, and I tell myself, okay, I need to learn this. So I start reading. And I start off fine. I read the first paragraph, I get the gist of it, I'm following along. 

But then... I don't know, maybe three or four minutes in, I'll suddenly realize that I'm at the bottom of the second page, and my eyes have been moving across the sentences the whole time, scanning every single line, but I didn't really take in a single word of what was written. My brain just completely checked out. It’s like the words just bounced right off my forehead, and I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. I have to scroll all the way back up to the top and start over, and sometimes I have to do that two or three times just to get through a basic update.

And it happens in those longer coaching meetings, too. My supervisor, Brenda—she’s a nice lady, she really is, but she has this very soft, kind of monotonous voice. And she’ll be going over my chat transcripts, talking about my resolution times, and I’m sitting there in her quiet little glass office, nodding my head, looking right at her... and then suddenly I realize I haven't actually processed anything she said for the last ten minutes. My ears are working, but I'm just not taking it in. I have to kind of shake myself and try to piece together what we were talking about, which is always a little embarrassing. So, yeah, if it's a long block of text or a long meeting where I'm just supposed to sit quietly and absorb information, I definitely lose the thread pretty quickly.
Do you find it hard to pay attention to details when you're working on a task?

Oh, boy, yeah. That’s... that’s definitely a thing for me. Details are just, well, they're kind of the bane of my existence sometimes. Like, I was talking about that Zendesk system earlier, right? The one corporate rolled out a few years ago? Well, when you finish a chat with a customer, you don't just say goodbye and close the window. There's this whole wrap-up process. It's a whole series of fields you have to fill out on the right-hand side of the screen before the system will let you go back into the pool. 

And I'll be sitting there, and I'll think, okay, great, handled that one perfectly, the customer is happy, I'm ready for the next one. So I hit submit. But then, maybe an hour later, or sometimes even the next day when I log in for my shift, the ticket gets kicked right back to my queue. And I'll open it up to look at it, and I'll realize... I don't know, I typed the wrong account number in the main field. Like, I transposed a 7 and a 9, or I just completely skipped the little drop-down box where you have to select the exact firmware version of the device they're calling about. Or I missed one little instruction from the new policy, like verifying the shipping address format. 

It's always just one little thing, but it makes the whole thing come back to me. And it's so frustrating because when it bounces back, it actually dings my quality score for the month. Brenda—my supervisor, the one with the soft voice I mentioned—she gets a notification about the rework every single time. I swear I'm looking right at the screen when I'm doing it, and I really do think I've finished the customer ticket completely, but my eyes just sort of skip right over those tiny details. I’ll fill out the customer's name, their email, the disposition code, but then I'll just breeze right past a required box. I know how to do it, I really do, and I know I need to slow down, but when I'm in the middle of a task, keeping track of every single little detail like that before moving on is just... it's a real struggle for me.
Do you often act on impulse in physical ways, such as intruding on others or grabbing things without thinking?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm going around grabbing things out of people's hands or anything like that. I'm not, you know, snatching staplers off desks or grabbing people's coffee mugs. But as far as intruding goes... yeah, I actually do that quite a bit. 

It’s mostly at work, honestly. See, they changed our office layout a couple of years ago. It used to be standard cubicles with the high walls where you had some real privacy, but then management decided to lower all the partitions to, I don't know, encourage a more "collaborative environment" or whatever the memo said. So now, you can hear pretty much everything going on around you, especially when it's a little slow on the chat queue. 

And the thing is, I’ve been there a while, right? I know the system, I know the policies inside and out. So if I’m sitting there and I hear one of my coworkers—like Dave, who sits to my left, or this newer girl, Chloe, on my right—if I hear them working through a customer problem and kind of talking it out loud or sighing because they're stuck on a tricky warranty issue... I just can't help myself. I don't mean to be rude at all, I really don't, but I'll just completely intrude on what they're doing. I'll roll my chair right over into their space or just lean right across the low partition and jump in with the answer before they’ve even finished their sentence. 

Like, they won't even have asked me for help. Nobody asked me a thing! They're just doing their job, maybe trying to figure it out on their own, and boom, there I am, inserting myself right into their business, telling them exactly what disposition code to use or how to handle the prorated refund. I just hear a problem and my brain immediately spits out the answer, and before I can stop myself or think, hey, maybe let them handle it, I'm already interrupting them. I know it probably drives them a little crazy, because sometimes people just want to learn by doing it themselves, you know? But I just... I just do it without even thinking about it. So, yeah, intruding on people, jumping into their conversations like that—that's definitely something I do without thinking.
Do you think your difficulties with focusing and impulsivity are more related to problems with paying attention or with controlling your physical activity and impulses?

Gosh, that's a... that's a really tough question to answer. Because, well, I don't really know. I mean, if you look at the reading thing and the meetings with Brenda, the attention part is obviously a huge problem. I sit there with those warranty updates and my brain just completely drifts off into space. But then, if you look at the physical part, the doing things without thinking, like rolling my chair over to Dave's desk to solve his ticket for him... that's just as big of a deal. 

So if you're asking me to weigh them against each other, or figure out if one causes the other... I honestly couldn't tell you. I've been working since I was eighteen, right out of high school, and it's always just been this big jumble for me. It's like... it's like a chicken and the egg kind of thing, you know? Am I interrupting Chloe because I can't focus on my own wrap-up codes, or can I not focus on my codes because my body is just too antsy and I feel this physical need to jump into her conversation? 

I sit there and try to parse it out in my head sometimes, especially after I mess up a ticket, and I just go in circles. My wife, she always tells me I'm just a busybody who tunes things out, which, well, she might have a point there. She says I've got a motor that won't quit but no steering wheel. But as far as which one is the real root of it all, or if the focus is more of a problem than the impulses... yeah, I really don't know. They just both seem to hit me all at once. I'm not sure how to separate them out like that.
Do you think your main struggle is with staying focused on tasks or with controlling your impulses to act or speak?

Well, like I was just saying a second ago, I really couldn't pick one over the other. It’s funny you ask it that way, though, because it really just feels like the exact same jumble I was just trying to describe to you. I honestly don't think I have a "main" struggle between the two, because they just tag-team me all day long. 

Like, just yesterday, I was trying to read this email from corporate about the new holiday PTO policy. It's this long email, right? Lots of bullet points, lots of dates you have to remember for blackout periods. And I just can't keep my eyes on it. I read the same paragraph three times and nothing sticks. That's the focus thing, obviously. But at the exact same time I'm struggling with that, Brenda walks by my desk carrying a box of those new headsets they've been promising us for months. And before she even sets the box down, before I even make a conscious decision to move, I'm already out of my chair, asking her if they have the noise-canceling feature, reaching into the box to look at the USB plug, completely interrupting a conversation she was having with the IT guy who was walking with her. 

So, I sit back down after that and I think... well, was my main problem right then that I couldn't focus on the PTO email, or was it that I couldn't stop myself from jumping up and grabbing a headset without asking? See what I mean? It's just all mashed together. I really couldn't tell you which one is the driver and which one is the passenger, so to speak. I don't know if the impulsivity is worse than the focus stuff, or if they just feed off each other. I just know they both happen, all the time, and I really couldn't separate them out to say one is the main issue.
Do you think your difficulties are more because you have trouble paying attention to things or because you have trouble controlling what you say and do?

Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here a little bit, because I really... I honestly don't have a different answer for you. I know you're trying to get me to pick a lane, to say, 'Oh, it's definitely the focus,' or 'It's definitely the blurting things out,' but like I was just saying, it's a total package deal for me. 

It's like asking if my left leg or my right leg is more responsible for me walking, you know? I've actually been sitting here trying to chew on it since you asked the first time, trying to see if maybe the attention thing is the real culprit. Like, maybe if I could just focus on my screen, I wouldn't be jumping into Chloe's conversations. But then I think about the times when I actually *am* dialed in. Like, say I'm on a call with a customer—maybe some nice lady from Ohio who's upset about a shipping delay—and I'm actually paying attention to her. I'm listening, I'm typing, I'm doing everything right. But then Dave drops a pen on his desk, or someone walks by with a squeaky shoe, and before the lady can even finish saying 'Toledo,' I'm spinning around, telling Dave he dropped his pen, completely interrupting the customer, losing my entire place in the billing system... 

So in that case, I *was* paying attention, but the impulse just totally hijacked my mouth and my body anyway. So which one is the main problem? I really, truly don't know. I wish I could give you a neat little breakdown, like, you know, sixty percent attention problems and forty percent impulse problems, but it's just one big messy soup in my head. They're tied for first place, as far as I can tell. I just don't have a clear answer for you on which one is the bigger issue.
Do you think your difficulties are more because you have trouble paying attention to things?

Look, Doc, I... I really feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again. Are you asking if it's *just* the attention part? Because, man, I've been trying to explain this, and I feel like maybe I'm not doing a good job, or maybe I'm using the wrong words. It's not *more* because of the attention. I just can't say that. 

I mean, I could sit here and tell you about the time last week when I was trying to read the updated manual on the new ticketing software—which, by the way, is a total nightmare, they moved all the drop-down menus to the left side of the screen, and don't even get me started on the font size they chose—and I was staring at the screen for maybe twenty minutes. Just staring. Reading the same sentence about "escalation protocols" over and over. And yeah, that's attention, right? That's me not being able to focus. 

But in that exact same twenty minutes, I also tapped my pen on the desk until it ran out of ink, I got up twice to check if the coffee pot was full even though I could see it from my desk and it was empty, and I blurted out a joke to Dave about the font size right when he was in the middle of a live chat with a platinum-tier customer. 

So, if you're asking me again if it's *more* the attention... I just don't know how to give you a different answer. It's not. It's both. It's the attention and the... the physical stuff, the blurting things out, the not being able to just sit still and do the thing I'm supposed to be doing. I can't separate them. I really can't. I'm sorry if that's not the answer you're looking for, but it's just the truth of how it is for me every single day.
Do you think your difficulties are causing you more problems in your daily life at work or in your personal relationships?

Well, that's... that's a really good question, actually. It's funny, because if you'd asked me that, say, five years ago, I might have said my personal life, you know, my relationships, because my wife used to get so frustrated with me constantly interrupting her stories or forgetting to take the trash out when I was right in the middle of a project in the garage. But lately? Lately, it's definitely the work stuff that's really starting to bite me. 

I've been a customer service rep for a long time, and I've always prided myself on being good with the customers. I mean, I really do get along with them. I can talk to anybody, calm them down when they're mad about a late shipment or a wrong order. That part comes naturally to me. But the actual... the machinery of the job, I guess you could call it, that's where I'm really hitting a wall, and it's starting to become a real problem. 

Like, it's actually showing up in my performance reviews now. My supervisor, Greg—nice guy, really, he's been with the company almost as long as I have—he pulled me into his office last month. And he sat me down and he had this whole printout of my metrics. And he pointed out all these unfinished tickets. Like, I'd start a ticket for a customer, get halfway through the notes, and then either I'd get distracted by another call coming in, or I'd go to look up a policy and end up reading some unrelated memo, and the ticket just sits there, open. 

And the mistakes, too. Just... silly, careless mistakes that I shouldn't be making at my age and with my experience. Typing in the wrong zip code, or forgetting to check the box for expedited shipping when the customer specifically asked for it. And Greg was saying, 'Look, you're great on the phone, the customers love you, but these errors... they're slowing the whole team down.' Because then someone else has to go in and fix my mess, or the customer calls back angry, and it just creates this whole bottleneck. And it's so frustrating, Doc, because I am trying. I'm really, really trying hard to stay on top of it, but it's like my brain just slips a gear right when I need it to hold steady. So, yeah, I'd have to say it's causing me a lot more grief at work right now than anywhere else. It's just... it's getting hard to hide it, you know?
Do you experience these difficulties with focusing and impulsivity in most areas of your life, or are they mainly limited to your work environment?

Well, gosh, everywhere? Most areas? I... I really don't know if I can say yes to that. I mean, I haven't exactly been keeping a logbook of my whole life, you know? 

Like I just mentioned with my wife, she used to get on my case about the interrupting and leaving things half-done in the garage a few years back, but... I don't really know if it's still happening all the time now, or if she just stopped mentioning it. We've been married for thirty-two years, so maybe she's just used to me being me at this point. And outside of home and work... I mean, what else is there, really? I go to the hardware store, I go to the grocery store. Am I impulsive in aisle four? I'm not sure. I haven't really noticed. I mean, sure, maybe I'll go in for a gallon of 2% milk and come out with a new brand of hickory barbecue sauce because the label looked interesting, but does that count? I figure everyone does that, right? 

Or with the focusing... like, if I'm sitting in my recliner watching a baseball game on a Sunday afternoon, I'm just watching the game. Or maybe I'm flipping channels between pitches. But is that a problem? I just don't know. Work is where the... the metrics are, you know? Like I was saying about Greg. He has that spreadsheet. He can literally point to a piece of paper and say, 'Here, you dropped the ball on this ticket, you messed up this zip code.' Nobody is handing me a spreadsheet for how I watched the Yankees game or how I mowed the lawn. 

So to answer your question... I really don't have a clue if it's happening in most areas of my life. I just haven't noticed it causing a ruckus anywhere else lately besides the call center. Without someone tracking my errors like they do at the office, I just... I really couldn't tell you one way or the other.
Do you experience difficulties with focusing and impulsivity at home or in social situations outside of work?

Well, if we're talking about home... I guess if I really stop and think about it, yeah, there is something that happens a lot. It’s the quiet stuff, you know? The things that are absolutely supposed to be relaxing after a long day on the phones. 

Like, take watching a movie with my wife. She loves those historical dramas, the ones with the long sweeping shots and the really slow talking. We've got this great sofa, bought it a couple of years ago, really good cushions, but I just... I can't just sit through a movie with her. It doesn't last long at all before I’m shifting around, trying to find a different position, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, tapping my foot on the coffee table. And then I start commenting on things, just blurting out whatever pops into my head, like "Why did they park that horse carriage there?" or "Hey, that guy was in that other cop show we watched, wasn't he?" And she’ll give me that look, you know, the "please just be quiet and watch" look. But I just can't help it. 

And then I end up getting up for something anyway. I'll go check if the back door is locked, or I'll go see if the dog needs to go out, even though he's fast asleep on his bed. I just have to get up and move. Same exact thing happens if I try to just sit and read at home. I used to love reading, I'll pick up a book, maybe a thriller that should be really gripping, but I'm just... I can't just sit quietly with it. I read a page and then I'm up adjusting the blinds, or going to the kitchen for a glass of water I don't really even want. 

So, yeah, I guess in those situations, the quiet ones where you're just supposed to relax and enjoy the evening, I really do struggle to just be still. It's like my motor is still running from dealing with customers all day, and I just can't turn the key off to sit still for a two-hour movie without driving my wife a little crazy with my pacing and talking.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, in school for sure, like I was saying, I’d just blurt things out. But honestly, it’s not just something from back then, it’s something I still do all the time right now at work. And I really, really don't mean to be rude, you know? I consider myself a polite person, I really do. But it's like... okay, for example, we have these pods at work now, right? With the new setup. So I can hear everything. And if I hear a couple of my coworkers, say, two desks over, and they're working through a complicated customer problem—maybe it's a billing issue, or a return that's outside the 30-day window, whatever it is—I can hear them struggling to figure out the protocol. 

And before I even realize I'm doing it, before I can stop myself, I just jump right in. I'll just call out the answer from my desk before they've even finished explaining the problem to each other, and definitely before anyone actually asked for my help. It’s like the answer just bubbles up in my throat and I have to get it out immediately. I can see them kind of jump, or look at me like, "We weren't talking to you," and I always feel terrible afterward because I know it comes off as intrusive or like I'm a know-it-all. But when it comes to actually *doing* things, like physical actions or intruding on people in other ways, I don't really see myself doing that. 

I mean, I'm trying to think of an example. Like, if someone is using the copier at work, I don't just walk up and push their papers out of the way to do mine, you know? I'll wait my turn. Or if someone is walking ahead of me in the hall, I don't just shove past them because I'm in a hurry. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to that one. It's really just the talking and the blurting things out that gets me into trouble. I just don't have that same kind of impulsive action when it comes to other things. It's kind of funny how that works, isn't it? doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulties with sustaining attention in tasks
doctor.question: Do you often find it hard to finish tasks or projects because you lose focus or get distracted?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: If a supervisor gives me three or four steps for a chat escalation, I usually do the first part and then somehow leave the notes or follow-up sitting there unfinished until someone reminds me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty finishing tasks or projects, which directly corresponds to failing to follow through on instructions and finish duties in the workplace.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. That's a huge thing for me, especially lately with this new setup at work. It's like... okay, so in customer service, especially when you're doing the online chats, which is mostly what I do now, there's a very specific way you're supposed to handle things when a customer gets angry or when the issue is beyond what a regular rep can authorize. We call it an escalation. 

So, say a supervisor comes over—or, well, messages me now, since we're in the pods—and gives me a rundown of what to do. They'll say, "Okay, first, issue the partial refund, then document the exact error code in the customer's main file, send an email to the logistics team to intercept the package, and finally, set a reminder to follow up with the customer in 48 hours." It's usually three or four steps like that, right? And I hear them, I really do, and I'll say, "Got it," and I dive right in. 

I'll get that partial refund processed immediately, no problem. I'm right on top of that first part. But then... I don't know what happens. It's like my brain just decides the crisis is averted because the customer is happy with the refund, or maybe another chat dings in and grabs my attention, or I just start thinking about what I'm going to have for lunch. Whatever it is, I just kind of... drift away from the rest of the instructions. 

I'll leave the file open on my screen, meaning to put the notes in, but then an hour goes by, and I haven't done it. The email to logistics? Forget it, it just completely falls out of my head. And the follow-up reminder never gets set. I just leave the whole back-end part of the process sitting there, completely unfinished. And it's not that I'm trying to be lazy or defiant, I just literally lose the thread of what I was supposed to be doing. I'll be working on three other things, thinking I'm doing a great job, until my supervisor messages me later and says, "Hey, did you ever finish documenting that escalation from this morning?" And then I get that sinking feeling in my stomach because I realize I only did the very first step and completely abandoned the rest of it. It happens all the time, and it's so frustrating because I know the steps, I just can't seem to hold my focus long enough to get through all of them before something else pulls me away.

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's actually kind of a running joke with some of the people I work with, though I guess it's probably not always that funny to them. But yeah, even when I’m really trying my best to just sit there and look completely calm and collected, my body is just... doing its own thing. 

Like, under my desk? My foot is just constantly bouncing. Up and down, up and down, like a little jackhammer. I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until I notice my monitors are sort of vibrating, or one of the other reps in the pod next to me gives me a look. And it's not just my feet, either. My hands are always looking for something to do. Like, whenever we have our team meetings—we do these weekly huddles in the conference room to go over our call metrics and new return policies and all that—I always bring a pen with me. You know, just in case I need to write something down, which I usually don't, but I have it anyway. And without even being aware of it, I'll just sit there clicking the top of the pen. Click, click, click. 

I'll be sitting there, looking right at the manager, thinking I look totally engaged and perfectly professional and still, but my thumb is just going to town on that pen. It's completely subconscious! Usually, it takes someone actually leaning over and whispering, "Hey, can you stop doing that?" for me to even realize I'm making a noise. It's just like my energy has to leak out somehow, you know? If I'm forced to just sit there in a chair for a twenty-minute meeting, my foot or my hands are going to find a way to keep moving, whether I want them to or not. I've tried sitting on my hands, or crossing my ankles really tight under the chair to lock my legs in place, but honestly, within five minutes I've uncrossed them and the foot is right back to bouncing again. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty waiting for their turn
doctor.question: Do you have trouble waiting for your turn in lines or when doing group activities?

target_item.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I do, actually. It's funny you ask that because it's something I've noticed a lot more lately with how things are structured at work now. You know, we have these team huddles, like I mentioned before, and then there's the help queue when we need a supervisor's assistance during a chat. And waiting... waiting is just really, really hard for me. It's like my skin starts to crawl, honestly. 

Take the team huddles, for example. The manager will go around the room, asking for updates or letting people share some kind of difficult customer interaction they had that week. And I know my turn is coming up. I know I'm like, third in line. But sitting there while the first two people are talking... I just get so antsy. I start shifting in my chair, and I can feel this pressure building up in my chest, like I just need to get my part out right that second. I catch myself almost leaning forward, opening my mouth, wanting to just jump in and say my piece before I'm even called on. I have to actively bite my tongue sometimes because the urge to just blurt out my update and be done with it is so strong. It's not that I don't care what my coworkers are saying, it's just the physical act of waiting my turn feels almost impossible sometimes.

And it's the same thing with the help queue on our chat system. When you have a really angry customer online and you need a supervisor to step in and authorize something big, you put your name in this digital queue. And you can see your spot. You're number four, then number three, then number two. And I will literally sit there, refreshing the screen, checking it over and over and over again. I know checking it doesn't make it go any faster, but I just can't stop myself. The customer is waiting, I'm waiting, and the whole time I'm just practically vibrating in my seat, staring at that little number on the screen, wishing I could just bypass the line and get what I need right then. It's just this overwhelming feeling of restlessness, like I can't just peacefully exist in a state of waiting. It has to happen now, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences emotional impulsivity
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself saying or doing things when you're upset that you later regret?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about saying or doing regrettable things when upset, which relates to emotional dysregulation or impulsivity, but this specific symptom is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I definitely get upset, don't get me wrong. You can't work in customer service for as many years as I have and not get upset. It's just the nature of the beast, right? Especially with the online chats we do now. People are so much braver when they're just typing at a screen instead of talking to a real human being on the phone. Just the other day, I had this guy—he bought one of our refurbished smart home hubs, the older model, not even the new one—and he was absolutely losing his mind because it wouldn't sync with his third-party security cameras. Which, if he had read the manual, it clearly states it doesn't support that anyway.

But anyway, he's typing all in caps, calling me every name in the book, telling me I'm useless and the company is a scam. And sure, my blood pressure goes up. I'm sitting there at my pod, and I can feel my face getting hot, and I'm definitely frustrated. But I don't... I don't actually lash out or type something back that I'd get fired for. I think after all these years, I've got this built-in filter for that kind of thing. I might take a deep breath, or maybe I'll mutter something under my breath to myself, like alright buddy whatever you say, but I don't actually say or do things I regret. I don't fly off the handle. I just type back the standard corporate response about understanding his frustration and looking for a resolution. 

Even outside of work, like with my wife or my neighbors. If I get mad, I usually just kind of withdraw a bit or go watch TV to cool down. I'm not really a yeller, and I don't have those moments where I just explode and then have to go apologize later because I said something terrible. I might be a lot of things, and I know I get distracted and fidgety like we were just talking about, but keeping my temper in check is actually something I'm pretty good at. I just let people vent and stick to the script, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty organizing tasks and activities
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble organizing your tasks and activities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty organizing tasks and activities, which corresponds to the ADHD symptom 'Organizing_Difficulty'. This symptom is not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Organizing? No, not really. Actually, that's one of the things I think I've got a pretty good handle on, to be honest. I mean, at work, it's all pretty much laid out for you anyway, so there's not much organizing I even have to do myself. We use this customer management system—it’s a customized version of Zendesk that corporate rolled out maybe three, three and a half years ago. Which, by the way, was a complete nightmare to learn at first because the old system had all our quick-reply macros right there on the left side of the screen, and the new one buried them in these tiny drop-down menus that you have to click three times just to find the standard shipping policy. 

But anyway, the system basically organizes my entire shift for me. The chats just come in automatically. Ping, ping, ping. I don't have to sit there and decide what task to do next or prioritize anything because the routing software does all that. You just take the next chat in the queue, help the customer, log the disposition code—you know, whether it was a return, or technical support, or just a billing question—and then you're right back in the pool for the next one. It’s very sequential, so I never really feel lost about what I'm supposed to be doing.

And then at home, I wouldn't say I struggle with it either. My wife, she’s a very organized person. Honestly, maybe a bit too organized sometimes, but it works for us. We have this big dry-erase calendar right on the front of the refrigerator, and she color-codes absolutely everything. Blue marker for doctor's appointments, red for when the utility bills are due, green for when our daughter is bringing the grandkids over. So if I ever need to know what I'm supposed to be doing on a Saturday afternoon, I just look at the fridge. Plus, I set all our regular bills up on autopay a few years back. That was probably one of the best decisions I ever made, honestly. I highly recommend it if you haven't done it yourself, it saves so much hassle with buying stamps and trying to remember due dates. 

So, yeah... I mean, maybe if I was trying to run my own business from scratch or had to plan some massive project with a hundred moving parts, I might get a little overwhelmed, but for my day-to-day life? No, I don't really have any trouble keeping my tasks straight. I just follow the queue at work and the whiteboard at home, and it all gets done.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with sustained attention in quiet activities
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to focus when you're reading or doing other quiet activities by yourself?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: In the longer coaching meetings or when I’m reading a new procedure, I start off fine but after a few minutes I realize my eyes kept moving and I didn’t really take in what was said.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty focusing during tasks like reading or other activities, which directly maps to the symptom of having trouble sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, that is something I struggle with. Especially at work. You know, we have these longer coaching meetings every month—they call them 'quality assurance reviews'—where they pull you off the queue for like, forty-five minutes to an hour to go over your metrics. And they also send out these massive emails whenever they change a policy. 

Like just last week, they completely revamped the warranty protocols for those smart home hubs I was telling you about earlier. So they send out this PDF, and it's maybe four or five pages long, just dense, tiny text about what qualifies for a free replacement and what doesn't, and all the new disposition codes we have to use. And I sit there at my desk, and it's quiet, right? Because I'm in an offline status to review it. And I open the document, and I tell myself, okay, I need to learn this. So I start reading. And I start off fine. I read the first paragraph, I get the gist of it, I'm following along. 

But then... I don't know, maybe three or four minutes in, I'll suddenly realize that I'm at the bottom of the second page, and my eyes have been moving across the sentences the whole time, scanning every single line, but I didn't really take in a single word of what was written. My brain just completely checked out. It’s like the words just bounced right off my forehead, and I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. I have to scroll all the way back up to the top and start over, and sometimes I have to do that two or three times just to get through a basic update.

And it happens in those longer coaching meetings, too. My supervisor, Brenda—she’s a nice lady, she really is, but she has this very soft, kind of monotonous voice. And she’ll be going over my chat transcripts, talking about my resolution times, and I’m sitting there in her quiet little glass office, nodding my head, looking right at her... and then suddenly I realize I haven't actually processed anything she said for the last ten minutes. My ears are working, but I'm just not taking it in. I have to kind of shake myself and try to piece together what we were talking about, which is always a little embarrassing. So, yeah, if it's a long block of text or a long meeting where I'm just supposed to sit quietly and absorb information, I definitely lose the thread pretty quickly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with sustaining attention in most tasks

patient.answer:
Oh, boy, yeah. That’s... that’s definitely a thing for me. Details are just, well, they're kind of the bane of my existence sometimes. Like, I was talking about that Zendesk system earlier, right? The one corporate rolled out a few years ago? Well, when you finish a chat with a customer, you don't just say goodbye and close the window. There's this whole wrap-up process. It's a whole series of fields you have to fill out on the right-hand side of the screen before the system will let you go back into the pool. 

And I'll be sitting there, and I'll think, okay, great, handled that one perfectly, the customer is happy, I'm ready for the next one. So I hit submit. But then, maybe an hour later, or sometimes even the next day when I log in for my shift, the ticket gets kicked right back to my queue. And I'll open it up to look at it, and I'll realize... I don't know, I typed the wrong account number in the main field. Like, I transposed a 7 and a 9, or I just completely skipped the little drop-down box where you have to select the exact firmware version of the device they're calling about. Or I missed one little instruction from the new policy, like verifying the shipping address format. 

It's always just one little thing, but it makes the whole thing come back to me. And it's so frustrating because when it bounces back, it actually dings my quality score for the month. Brenda—my supervisor, the one with the soft voice I mentioned—she gets a notification about the rework every single time. I swear I'm looking right at the screen when I'm doing it, and I really do think I've finished the customer ticket completely, but my eyes just sort of skip right over those tiny details. I’ll fill out the customer's name, their email, the disposition code, but then I'll just breeze right past a required box. I know how to do it, I really do, and I know I need to slow down, but when I'm in the middle of a task, keeping track of every single little detail like that before moving on is just... it's a real struggle for me.

doctor.question: Do you often act on impulse in physical ways, such as intruding on others or grabbing things without thinking?

target_item.name: Interrupting_Intruding
target_item.manifestation: I don’t mean to be rude, but if I hear coworkers working through a customer problem, I’ll jump in with an answer before they’ve finished or before anyone asked me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intruding on others or acting impulsively by grabbing things, which matches the symptom of interrupting or intruding on others.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't say I'm going around grabbing things out of people's hands or anything like that. I'm not, you know, snatching staplers off desks or grabbing people's coffee mugs. But as far as intruding goes... yeah, I actually do that quite a bit. 

It’s mostly at work, honestly. See, they changed our office layout a couple of years ago. It used to be standard cubicles with the high walls where you had some real privacy, but then management decided to lower all the partitions to, I don't know, encourage a more "collaborative environment" or whatever the memo said.
